title: Bertie's Moon Race
markdown:
Bertie the bunny loved his special stones. He put them in order in his cozy home. Outside, Waffle the wombat munched a yummy carrot. The sun, a big orange ball, was getting sleepy. It painted the sky soft peachy colours.

Suddenly Bertie hopped out of his home. Fluffy ears twitched. He was tidying his books and found one hidden away. It was called The Whispering Woods. On the back, a little red stamp winked.

“Oh dear, oh me, oh my.” Whiskers trembled a little. “This book is very, very, very late.”

Waffle stopped munching. Nose wrinkled. “Late?” His voice like soft stones rolling.

“Yes.” Bertie hopped closer, holding the book carefully. “The book wagon only comes once a week. And it leaves when the moon is bright and high. Look.” He pointed a small paw. A sliver of moon, like a shy smile, was peeking out. “The moon will be big and round very soon. If the book is late, the book lady, Mrs. Winkle, will be sad.”

Bertie’s ears drooped a little. He didn’t want Mrs. Winkle to be sad. His nose wiggled.

Waffle finished his carrot and patted Bertie’s paw. “Don’t worry, Bertie. We can take it back. We can be really, really fast.”

Bertie’s eyes lit up. “A race. A race against the moon. What an adventure.” He hopped up and down. “Come on, Waffle. Let’s go.”

We’re going, we’re going.

Bertie tucked The Whispering Woods safely under his arm. They set off. The path had sleepy flowers closing their petals. Soft grass tickled their feet. The moon climbed higher, shining a gentle silvery light.

“We’re going, we’re going,” Bertie puffed, taking big excited hops.
“We’re going, we’re going,” Waffle walked along next to him. His little tail gave a happy wag.

Soon they came to a little stream. It gurgled and babbled happily. Too wide for Bertie to hop. The water looked cool and splashy. Bertie’s nose wiggled. “How will we get over?”

Waffle looked at the stream. He looked at Bertie’s worried face. A happy rumble. “Easy peasy, Bertie. My waddle is perfect for streams.” He stepped into the water. It came up to his round tummy. He made himself a little bridge with his strong back. “Hop on, friend.”

Bertie giggled. He held the book tight and hopped onto Waffle’s back. “Thank you. You’re a brilliant bridge.” Waffle waddled across steadily. Plish-plash went his feet. The stream seemed to giggle with them.

On the other side the path was trickier. The moon was a big happy circle, shining bright. They came to soft glowy flowers that looked like moonlight. When they tried to walk, the flowers wobbled and bounced them. “Moon-petals,” Bertie whispered. The more they stepped, the more they bounced. The book almost tumbled.

Waffle stopped. A surprised chuckle. “They’re tickly and wobbly.”

Bertie looked around. He spotted a clearer patch of grass that curved around the wobbly flowers. “Waffle. Look. If we go this way, around the wobbly bits, we can sneak past.”

Waffle looked where Bertie pointed. “A clever path.” They tiptoed carefully. The flowers swayed like friendly dancers. The moon watched with a bright smile.

We’re going, we’re going.

Now they saw the book wagon, a little wooden house on wheels. A warm lantern hung from its door. Mrs. Winkle, the book lady, was just closing up.

“Hurry, hurry,” Bertie urged, bunny feet a blur.
“Almost there, almost there,” Waffle panted, his waddle turning into a quick pace.

They reached the wagon just as Mrs. Winkle was closing the door. The moon was at the very top of the sky, a perfect shining circle.

“We made it.” Bertie held out the book with pride.
Mrs. Winkle smiled a wide warm smile. “Well, hello there, Bertie and Waffle. Just in time. And what a wonderful adventure you must have had to bring The Whispering Woods back so carefully.” She took the book. “Thank you for being good readers.”

Bertie and Waffle puffed out their chests. A warm glow spread through them. They had helped each other.

“We did it,” said Bertie, giving Waffle a happy nudge.
“We did it,” echoed Waffle, giving Bertie a gentle hug.

The moonbeams twinkled brighter. They turned to head home. The journey back felt even cozier. Bertie’s friendship with Waffle shone as bright as the moon itself. We’re going, we’re going — home this time, book returned, moon still watching.
